claims.text: Low hardness and strength in equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi solid-solution alloys are governed by facile dislocation glide.
A relatively low effective stacking-fault energy contributes to facile dislocation glide in CoCrFeNiTi.
Modest lattice distortion in CoCrFeNiTi minimizes dislocation pinning and work hardening.
The simple solid-solution state is dominated by mobile dislocations with weak mutual interactions and few intrinsic obstacles.
Facile dislocation motion explains the combination of high plasticity and machinability with low resistance to plastic flow.
The starting material is equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a single-phase solid-solution state with relatively coarse, undeformed grains.
Severe plastic deformation will increase dislocation density and may produce a nanostructured microstructure.
Minor boron doping can form nanoscale precipitates at grain boundaries in this alloy.
The comparison will use otherwise identical treated and untreated samples tested at room temperature and quasi-static strain rates.
Increased dislocation density, refined grain boundaries, or nanoscale precipitates will impede free dislocation motion.
Low intrinsic lattice distortion and low effective stacking-fault energy allow dislocations to nucleate and glide without forming immobilizing networks.
The intervention will generate additional dislocation interactions or precipitate obstacles that raise the barrier to dislocation motion.
Intervention-treated material will have higher hardness and yield strength than untreated material because of enhanced dislocation pinning.
The pristine material will exhibit low yield stress and minimal work hardening.
The treated samples will exhibit a marked increase in flow stress and hardness.
As-cast or homogenized equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has good plasticity and machinability but low hardness and yield strength at room temperature under quasi-static loading.

The proposed mechanism applies only to single-phase CoCrFeNiTi at room temperature and quasi-static strain rates and may not apply at high temperatures, very high strain rates, or in multiphase microstructures.
Twinning or subtle phase transformations may contribute to deformation but are expected to be secondary under the specified conditions.

Failure to observe a statistically significant strength or hardness increase together with failure to observe increased interactions or obstructive microstructural changes is defined as falsifying the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis is bounded to a single-phase solid-solution state, but the doping branch deliberately introduces precipitates or secondary phases, placing the treated material outside that stated boundary.
